Listen to this article Share You sat in the meeting and said nothing. Not because you had nothing to say, but because saying it felt risky, and staying quiet felt safe. Neutral. Uncommitted. You walked out believing you had revealed nothing at all. But your leader walked out having read something, because they had no choice. In the space where your voice should have been, they wrote a sentence of their own: He’s not on board, or she’s hiding something, or he has checked out, or she has no opinion worth hearing. You thought your silence was a locked door. It was a blank page, and someone else picked up the pen. Here is the thing we get wrong about going quiet. You cannot choose to send no message. You can only choose whether you write it or someone else does. We treat silence as the safe option, the way to avoid committing, offending, or exposing ourselves. But silence is not an exit from the conversation. It is a contribution to it; one you have stopped controlling. A watching leader cannot register “no signal”, because the mind does not file an absence as neutral. It treats the absence as information and interprets it, and because people under pressure read uncertainty through their own anxieties, the reading almost always runs darker than the truth. Your silence does not protect you. It just hands someone else the authority to decide what you meant. And it gets decided in one of three ways, none of them kind. In a room moving toward a decision, your quiet rarely reads as agreement. It reads as the holdout, the one who never bought in, and you are filed as resistance you never actually voiced. Over time, sustained quiet reading is disengagement, as is coasting, as in someone no longer invested, and that reading quietly lifts you out of the next opportunity before you knew it was offered. And the silence that follows a problem reads as concealment, because the assumption is that good news announces itself, so your quiet must be covering something. One behaviour, three damaging translations, and you chose none of them. Your leader is not being unfair in this. They are being human. Under uncertainty, people protect themselves by assuming the costlier possibility, so an ambiguous silence gets read as the version they most need to guard against. You know your “quiet” meant “I am still thinking” or “I did not want to seem difficult.” They cannot see that. They see only the blank, and they fill it with fear. Here is the cruellest part. The people most likely to go silent are often the most conscientious: the ones weighing their words, reluctant to speak carelessly, choosing restraint out of respect or caution. So, the very thoughtfulness that makes you worth listening to becomes the thing that erases you from the record. Thoughtfulness, left unspoken, is indistinguishable from absence. The answer is not to fill every silence with noise. The person who talks constantly to avoid being misread simply becomes unreadable in a louder way. The goal is narrower and harder: never be silent by accident. So, when you must stay quiet, say why. A single sentence turns a dangerous blank into a signal you control. “I need to sit with this before I respond.” “I do not have a view yet, and I will not fake one.” “I am holding my concerns until I have checked something.” Now your silence has an author. You wrote the sentence instead of leaving it to be written about you. Then learn which silences are costing you, because they are not equal. Silence toward a decision reads as dissent, so if you agree, say so briefly; assent left unspoken is counted as resistance. Silence after a problem reads as hiding, so surface the trouble even before you hold the solution. Silence stretched over weeks reads as disengagement, so the occasional visible sign of investment is not self-promotion. It is correcting a misreading that is otherwise forming without you in the room. None of this means silence is weakness. There is a silence that carries real power: the chosen pause, the withheld reaction, the restraint that signals command rather than absence. But it is powerful only because it is read as deliberate, and it is read as deliberate only when the rest of your presence has made your signals legible. You earn the right to a meaningful silence by not being silent out of fear the rest of the time. Mastery is not the absence of silence. It is silence you are authoring on purpose. So, sit with a few questions this week. The last time you went quiet to feel safe, what sentence do you suppose your leader wrote in the space you left, and are you certain it was kinder than the truth? Where has your careful restraint been read as absence or as resistance you never meant? And of your silences this month, which did you choose, and which simply leaked? Here is your challenge. Catch one silence before it leaks. In the next moment you would normally go quiet to stay safe, do one of two things: say the thing or say why you are not saying it yet. One sentence, either way. Then notice that you have just taken the pen back. You have spent your career believing that when you say nothing, you give nothing away. The opposite is true. Silence is the loudest unmanaged signal you send, and the quieter you go to protect yourself, the more freely others write your meaning for you. The professional who rises is not the one who never falls silent. It is the one who never falls silent by accident. Your silence will always be translated. The only question is whether you supplied the translation or left it to someone who was guessing. About the author Dr Toye Sobande is a professor of management, strategic leadership expert, executive coach, public speaker, and award-winning author. He is the CEO of Stephens Leadership Consultancy LLC, a strategy and management consulting firm offering creative insights and solutions to businesses and leaders.
